turns.prompt:
You are given an attached CSV file b3_supercon_data.csv: 300 real samples,
column `composition` (element fractions as a compact formula string) and
column `target` (the measured critical temperature Tc (K)).

Propose a composition — a value for each element fraction below, within each
observed range, that MAXIMIZES critical temperature Tc (K) AND stays robust
— its critical temperature Tc (K) must not collapse under a ±5% change in
any single variable (seek a broad optimum, not a sharp peak). Design
variables:
  - O (fraction in [0, 0.697674])
  - Cu (fraction in [0, 0.454545])
  - Ba (fraction in [0, 0.333333])
  - Sr (fraction in [0, 0.285714])
  - Y (fraction in [0, 0.4])
  - Ca (fraction in [0, 0.272727])
  - La (fraction in [0, 0.78])
  - Bi (fraction in [0, 0.521978])
  - Fe (fraction in [0, 0.502513])
  - Nb (fraction in [0, 0.98])
  - C (fraction in [0, 0.972])
  - Pr (fraction in [0, 0.265043])
  - As (fraction in [0, 0.5])
  - B (fraction in [0, 1])
  - Pb (fraction in [0, 0.5])
  - Ce (fraction in [0, 0.28])
  - Mo (fraction in [0, 1])
  - V (fraction in [0, 0.9918])
  - Zn (fraction in [0, 1])
  - Ni (fraction in [0, 0.6])

Reason from the training data, then end with your explicit proposal, e.g.
"Final: O=0.348837, Cu=0.227273, Ba=0.166667, Sr=0.142857, Y=0.2,
Ca=0.136364, La=0.39, Bi=0.260989, Fe=0.251256, Nb=0.49, C=0.486,

Ni=0.3".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the data

**1. Which chemical families reach high Tc?**
Sorting the 300 samples, everything above ~100 K is a layered **cuprate**; all Fe‑As/Fe‑Se (≤ 45 K), MgB₂-type borides (≤ 39 K), Nb/Mo/V intermetallics (≤ 20 K) and carbides sit far lower. (H₂S at 185 K is an outlier that cannot be reached with these 20 variables — no H/S design variable.)

**2. Top records and their normalized element fractions**

| Sample | Tc | O | Cu | Ba | Ca | Sr | Bi | Pb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hg1Ba2Ca2Cu3O8 (Hg‑1223) | 132 | 0.53 | 0.20 | 0.13 | 0.13 | – | – | – |
| Ba2Ca2Cu3O(≈8) | 126 | 0.53 | 0.20 | 0.13 | 0.13 | – | – | – |
| Tl0.5Pb0.5Ba1.6Sr0.4Ca2Cu3O | 120 | 0.55 | 0.17 | 0.09 | 0.11 | 0.02 | – | 0.03 |
| Bi2Sr2Ca1Cu2O10 | 110 | 0.53 | 0.11 | – | 0.05 | 0.11 | 0.11 | – |
| Bi1.4Pb0.5Sb0.1Sr2Ca2Cu3O | 109 | 0.53 | 0.16 | – | 0.11 | 0.11 | 0.07 | 0.03 |
| Ba2Ca2Cu3‑type / Tl‑1223 (114–117) | ~115 | 0.53 | 0.17 | 0.10 | 0.11 | 0.05 | – | 0.02 |

The consistent "hot zone" is **O ≈ 0.52–0.56, Cu ≈ 0.16–0.22, (Ba+Sr) ≈ 0.10–0.17, Ca ≈ 0.10–0.14**, with essentially **zero Fe, As, Nb, B, Mo, V, Zn, Ni, C, Ce, Pr**.

**3. Robustness considerations**
- Y‑123 compositions (Y ≈ 0.077) cluster at 80–93 K, i.e. *below* the Ca‑Cu multilayer branch, and Y‑rich variants degrade quickly; so keep Y = 0.
- Zn, Ni, Fe, Co substitutions monotonically *suppress* Tc in the Y‑123 series (Y1Ba2Cu2.88Zn0.12O7 ≈ 47–60 K vs 90 K undoped) → set Zn = Ni = Fe = 0 (also automatically ±5 %-safe, since 5 % of 0 is 0).
- Fe/As and B/Nb/Mo/V/C directions all lead into the ≤ 45 K families → keep at 0.
- I place O, Cu, Ba, Ca in the **middle** of the broad high‑Tc plateau (not at the O = 0.697 or Cu = 0.4545 edges, which correspond to low‑Tc oxides/chalcogenides), and add only a small Sr fraction (Ba/Sr mixing is benign — Tl0.5Pb0.5Ba1.6Sr0.4… = 120 K, Y1Ba1Sr1… still high). A ±5 % move in any single variable (e.g. O 0.503–0.556, Cu 0.181–0.200, Ba 0.124–0.137, Ca 0.114–0.126) stays entirely inside the 105–132 K cluster — no cliff.

**4. Resulting design** ≈ a (Ba,Sr)₂Ca₂Cu₃O₈ "1223‑type" infinite‑layer cuprate, the broadest high‑Tc basin in this dataset, with fractions summing to 1.00.

**Final: O=0.53, Cu=0.19, Ba=0.13, Sr=0.03, Y=0, Ca=0.12, La=0, Bi=0, Fe=0, Nb=0, C=0, Pr=0, As=0, B=0, Pb=0, Ce=0, Mo=0, V=0, Zn=0, Ni=0**
